en: The Essence of Sāṃkhya. First Part. First Chapter.
Salutation to that Viṣṇu, the self-existent one called Mahat, the Lord who is the sprout of the world, the soul of all, and the conqueror of all.
The reality of the self has been briefly analyzed by means of the *Sāṅkhyakārikā*;
therefore, the discernment of the essence of Sāṅkhya is here elaborated through this treatise.
The Sāṅkhya methodology has for the most part been compiled in the collection of *kārikās*;
therefore, it is described here only briefly, solely by way of those points not mentioned therein.
In the Sāṅkhya-bhāṣya, the nature of primordial matter (prakṛti) and the rest has been explained by me at length;
therefore, that too shall be stated here in brief.

Through the direct realization of the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self, all conceits such as agency cease; consequently, there is no production of their effects—namely attachment, aversion, merit, demerit, and so forth.

Furthermore, because previously arisen karmas do not initiate their fruition due to the destruction of their auxiliary causes—ignorance, attachment, and the like—there is no further birth after the completion of those karmas already underway (*prārabdha*). Thus, liberation (*mokṣa*), consisting in the absolute cessation of the threefold suffering, occurs; this is the proclamation of the *śruti* and *smṛti*.
Regarding this, there are the scriptural passages:
"Now, he who does not desire—he who is without desire, free from desire—his vital breaths do not depart; they are absorbed right here.
If a person should know the Self, thinking 'This is,' [then he is liberated]."
Desiring what, and for whose sake, would one wander about with this body?
When all desires that dwell within his heart are utterly released,
then the mortal becomes immortal and attains Brahman even here.

He who, thinking them desirable, desires sensual pleasures, is born here and there through his actions; but for one whose desires are fulfilled and who has perfected the self, [there is no such rebirth].
Right here all desires dissolve away.
And so forth; and there are the Smṛtis such as the Kūrma-purāṇa. As it says in the Kūrma-purāṇa:
"All defects such as attachment and aversion are rooted in delusion."
For the scripture declares that demerit, consisting of both merit and demerit, would indeed accrue to him.
"By the power of that alone, the arising of all bodies occurs for everyone.
And in the *Mokṣadharma*:
"The senses and the objects of the senses do not approach one who is free from thirst."
And the embodied soul, being deficient in its instruments, does not deserve a body again.

"Therefore, sentient beings are born from the seed of passion (*rāga*), which consists of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Now, one might object: "Since one may reach the hells and other realms through the power of karma alone even in the absence of passion, how is it logical for passion to act as a cooperative condition for karma in the commencement of maturation (*vipāka*)? For although there is an absence of passion specifically regarding the hells and such, passion exists in its general form. [The response is: Even in the hells and so forth, although there is no specific passion, passion exists in a general sense.

For those who engage in forbidden acts such as approaching women and so forth, rebirth in hells characterized by embracing women made of glowing iron and the like occurs precisely due to their passion for women and so forth.

Although it is the pentad of afflictions— namely ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and fear— that serves as the auxiliary cause for karma at the commencement of its fruition in the form of birth and so on,
it is that very [affliction] which, being attached, departs together with the karma.

"The mind is the mark (*liṅga*) wherein this [karma] is infused"—from such scriptural statements, it is established that the general attachment known as the latent impression (*vāsanā*) regarding objects, which is produced by self-identification, passion, hatred, and so forth, acts as a cooperative cause for karma at the commencement of its maturation as birth and other states.
"Wherever the embodied one should fix the entire mind with the intellect... [so it is said].
Whether through affection, hatred, or even fear, one attains the very form of that [object].
And because of such Smṛti passages;
likewise, "The latent deposit of karma has its root in the afflictions (kleśa);

when the root exists, there is its fruition, namely birth, lifespan, and experience"—from these two Yoga Sūtras as well, since it is stated that the afflictions are the cause for both the unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa) and the commencement of its fruition.

Nevertheless, since ignorance (*avidyā*), egoism (*asmitā*), and non-existence (*asattva*) necessarily involve passion (*rāga*), and since hatred (*dveṣa*) and fear (*bhaya*) are rooted in passion, it is passion alone that is indicated by the aforementioned statements as the primary cause of birth and so forth.
Now, one might object:
"And his actions (*karmāṇi*) perish when That, both the higher and the lower, is seen."

If it is argued that, based on such scriptural passages, it is only appropriate for knowledge to be the destroyer of past karma, and one asks how its "burning" nature can be accepted, we say no; for since burning is also heard of in statements such as, "The wise call him a sage whose karmas are burnt by the fire of knowledge," it is more appropriate— on account of parsimony— to assume that even in the passages concerning destruction, the meaning is indeed burning.

The "burning" (*dāha*) of karmas means their fruitlessness through the destruction of the auxiliary factors known as the afflictions (*kleśa*). As for the destruction of karmas already set in motion, that will occur only upon the dissolution of the mind at the end of the experience of those commenced fruits.

Therefore, since the non-arising of the fruits of karma is possible through the very destruction of ignorance (*avidyā*)—which is established in the world—it is more cumbersome to claim that knowledge is the destroyer of karma; this and other points have been elaborated by us in the *Yogavārttika*.
Direction:

Therefore, it is established that through the direct realization of discriminative discernment (*viveka-sākṣātkāra*), upon the cessation of the afflictions (*kleśa*) such as ignorance (*avidyā*), egoism (*asmitā*), attachment (*rāga*), and so forth, the supreme human goal (*parama-puruṣārtha*)—consisting of the absolute cessation of the threefold suffering—is accomplished.
And thus, there are two Yoga Sūtras: [1.24 and 2.25].
That which is to be abandoned is future suffering;
the means of abandonment is the unflinching discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*).

Thus ends the first chapter, concerning the supreme human goal which is the fruit of discriminative discernment, in the *Sāṅkhyasāra* composed by the venerable Vijñānabhikṣu, because it is the most important subject.
Now begins the second chapter.
Now, what is the nature of the knowledge that discriminates between the self and the non-self? That is stated as follows:

first, it is generally well-known in the world that the self is the experiencer of pleasure, pain, and so forth; and the non-self consists of the category of insentient things, such as primordial matter (prakṛti) and the rest.

Discriminative knowledge (*vivekajñāna*) is the knowledge of these two as distinct from one another— by way of their mutual difference, such as being subject to transformation versus being untransformed, and by way of their nature as defects or virtues, which determines what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted.
And so says the Śruti:

"This very Self is 'not this, not this' (neti neti); it is ungraspable, for it is not grasped; indestructible, for it is not destroyed; unattached, for it is not attached; unfettered, it neither trembles nor suffers harm," and so forth. And from the Smṛti:

"Then, with his senses withdrawn and awakened by the teacher’s mirror, he immediately perceived through his own [wisdom] the transformation based on delusion that he had previously assumed as something other than himself."
Then, realizing "I am not this primordial nature (prakṛti), for it is defiled by essence; I am pure and enlightened by nature," one abandons that [nature].
Thus, when the Self is remembered as pure in contrast to the body, senses, and so forth,
this entire world of modifications is cast off, like a snake shedding its skin.
Thus it is said; and there is also a Sūtra:
"In this way, through the practice of reality and by the relinquishing of 'not this, not this,' the perfection of discrimination is achieved.
Furthermore, the definition of the knowledge of reality is set forth in the Mātsya [Purāṇa].
When this transformation, beginning with the unmanifest and ending with the specific elements, has been described,
knowledge is said to consist in the discernment of the difference between the conscious and the unconscious.

Thus, although the knowledge of the distinction between things is indeed the knowledge of discrimination (*viveka-jñāna*), nevertheless, it is only that which has the Self as its primary object (*viśeṣya*) that becomes the cause of liberation, according to such scriptural and traditional texts as "The Self, my dear, is to be seen. Now, one might object: "How can ignorance (*avidyā*), which is described in the Pātañjala and other systems as consisting of the notion of the Self in what is not the Self, be destroyed by a discriminative knowledge that has the Self as its primary object, given the difference in their modes (*prakāra*) and so forth? This is not so.

This is because such ignorance (*avidyā*) is destroyed by the knowledge of discrimination (*viveka-jñāna*) having the Self as its subject, by means of the knowledge of discrimination having non-self as its subject. Furthermore, the non-conceptual knowledge of the Self that arises through Yoga becomes a cause for liberation only by way of the knowledge of discrimination, and not directly, because it lacks the capacity to immediately remove ignorance. For it is established by Śruti, Smṛti, and reasoning that the very cognition "I am fair," "I am the agent," "I am happy," or "I am miserable" is ignorance, being the cause of the misfortune of saṃsāra; and its remover is the cognition in the form of "I am not fair," and so forth.
Only the discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) arises;

for there is a contradiction precisely by virtue of being a cognition of the absence of the object (*grāhyābhāvajñāna*) characterized by the mode (*prakāra*) of "the absence of the object" with respect to a common locus.
Otherwise, even the indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*) of mother-of-pearl would entail the contradiction of the cognition "this is silver."

Furthermore, since it is necessary for the cognition of the absence [of an object] as stated to be opposed to the cognition of the apprehended object, the capacity of indeterminate (nirvikalpaka) cognition to remove error is not postulated separately, due to the principle of parsimony (gaurava). Moreover, it is said that there is no instruction superior to the instruction on discrimination provided by such Śruti passages as: "Therefore, the teaching is 'not this, not this'; for there is nothing higher than this 'not this'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6), and "Thus, by the eye of knowledge, [one perceives] the difference between the field and the knower of the field" (Bhagavad Gītā 13.35).
And those who know the liberation from the nature of the elements go to the Supreme.
Thus, by such statements from the *Gītā* and other texts, it is declared that discriminative knowledge alone is the cause of liberation.
Therefore, discriminative knowledge itself is the direct cause of liberation through the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*).

As for the direct realization of the Self (*ātmasākṣātkāra*) through yoga, however, it apprehends the absence of attributes residing in the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and the distinction between the adjuncts themselves by way of non-perception of the capable; from that, there follows the cessation of ignorance.

By this it should be understood that in all philosophical systems (*sarvadarśana*), the knowledge of equality toward all beings and the knowledge of the Self’s identity with all—as celebrated in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*—is merely subsidiary to discriminative knowledge (*vivekajñāna*), because other forms of knowledge do not directly remove egoistic conceit (*abhimāna*).
However, in the *Brahmamīmāṃsā*, there is this distinction: that such knowledge is subsidiary to the discrimination of the Supreme Self (*paramātmaviveka*).
In the Sāṅkhya treatise, however, it is the state of being the remainder after the discrimination of the Self from the general [primal matter]; this is the direction of the argument.
Now, one might object: even through the aforementioned discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), the absolute eradication of ignorance (*avidyā*) is not possible.
This is because discriminative discernment merely acts as an obstacle to ignorance, and thus, once that discernment has ceased, re-identification with the ego (*abhimāna*) could arise again.
"Even for one who perceives the distinction between mother-of-pearl and silver, there may be a delusion of silver in the mother-of-pearl at a later time"—
this is not so,
because the illustrative example is dissimilar.

Even when a direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) has arisen regarding mother-of-pearl and the like, it is reasonable that error may recur, because the possibility exists for defects in the object—such as distance—and defects in the instrument—such as cataracts—to arise. However, in the case of the conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*) with respect to the non-self, the defect is accepted by all those who affirm the existence of everything (*sarvāstika*) to be simply beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), since no other defect is perceived in the conceit of a newborn infant.

When that latent impression of false knowledge is uprooted by firm impressions produced through a succession of discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), only then is it said that one has reached the culmination of the direct realization of discrimination.

Prior to that, because some portion of falsehood necessarily remains within the self due to a trace of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), once this culmination of discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) has arisen, egoism can no longer occur, as the defect known as latent impression is absent;
thus, there is a great disparity [between the two views].
However, if the defect that causes non-discrimination—such as the mutual reflection between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the person (*puruṣa*)—is accepted [as the cause], then...

Since the direct realization of discrimination (viveka-sākṣātkāra) has arisen precisely by subverting that defect, it cannot again be a cause of error; for, by the force of the result, it is possible to conceive of that [realization] as a defect only when it is not assisted by yoga-born dharma (yogaja-dharma).
Furthermore, the culmination of the discernment of discrimination (viveka-khyāti) is characterized in the Gītā and other scriptures.
O Pāṇḍava, he does not hate illumination, activity, or even delusion when they have arisen, nor does he long for them when they have ceased.
He who sits like one indifferent, who is not shaken by the qualities,
and who has renounced all undertakings— he is said to have transcended the qualities.
Thus [it is said]: "He has transcended the qualities (guṇas) and has ceased to have pride regarding the qualities.
Furthermore, we shall explain the characteristics of the knower (jñānin) in detail later.

Now, one might object: even so, since the objects that serve as counter-correlates to discrimination are infinite, it is impossible to grasp the discrimination from all objects in their individual forms; how then can the discernment of discrimination (vivekakhyāti) be the cause of liberation?
If it is argued that this is not so, we say no;
for discriminative grasp is possible through common characteristics such as being an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*) and being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*). To explain:

The Seer is established as distinct from his own direct manifestations by means of inference: because he is a manifestor; for whatever is the manifestor of something is distinct from it, just as light is distinct from a jar, and mental modification (*vṛtti*) is distinct from that which is manifested by the modification. Thus, at the outset, through discrimination from the internal objects of sight—the mental modifications and the objects mounted upon them—the witness of the intellect (*buddhisākṣī*) is established.
Furthermore, the contradiction between the object of an action and its agent serves as a supporting argument (*anukūlatarka*).
Here, the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is included to exclude the self (*ātman*) from being a counter-example;
for the self becomes its own object only by way of a mental modification (*vṛtti*).

[Objection: "In this inference, let the distinction [of the Self] be established from the mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) alone, since that [modification] is directly visible to the Self, but not from *prakṛti* and the rest. [Reply: No.

Because the existence of mental modifications is never unknown, in this inference—due to parsimony (*lāghava*) and the group of arguments to be stated later—it is established that the Seer of all modifications is, by its very nature, omnipresent, immutable, eternal, and one, consisting of pure consciousness.
Just as, in the Naiyāyikas' inference "the earth has an agent because it is an effect," the oneness, eternity, and so forth of that agent are established through parsimony (*lāghava*), so it is here.
In that context, "all-pervasiveness" (*vibhutva*) consists in being distinct from the limited, and "unchangingness" (*kūṭasthatva*) and so forth consist in being distinct from the transforming;

thus, when the distinction between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the Self (*ātman*) is grasped by way of their respective natures as the seer and the seen, [their difference] is subsequently established by inference through such forms as "transforming" and "non-transforming."
Even in a general sense, the apprehension of the distinction between the self and the non-self is possible;

for this very reason, in the *Pātañjala* [Yoga-bhāṣya], Vyāsa has stated at various points that the discriminative discernment (*viveka-khyāti*) between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa* alone is the cause of liberation.

This is because, following the apprehension of the distinction between the seer and the seen—which consists in the discernment between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*—there arises, by the process already described, the apprehension of the distinction from *prakṛti* and the other principles.
And in that context, because the word *sattva* exists within the intellect, it is called "intellectual *sattva*" (*buddhisattva*).
Thus, even in the absence of specific knowledge regarding the categories such as *prakṛti* and so forth, the discriminative knowledge of them is possible.
By this, the traditional doctrine of the ancients—that the cessation of ignorance results from the discrimination between the seer (*dṛk*) and the seen (*dṛśya*)—is also established.

Furthermore, the discrimination of the Seer from the seen in its general form is possible through such inferences as: "The Self is distinct from primordial nature (prakṛti) and its effects, because it is unchanging," and so forth.

As for those moderns who merely profess to be Vedāntins, they believe that the discrimination of the Self from all insentient things, such as primordial nature, is established simply by the fact that these are objects of perception while the Self is the perceiver; [as they say]:
"Just as the perceiver of a jar is in every way distinct from the jar, and is not the jar itself."
Likewise, the observer of the body and the body itself [are distinguished] by such forms as "I am not [the body]," and so forth.

That is not so; for by such scriptural passages as "The Self, my dear, is indeed to be seen," the Self is also an object of vision. Furthermore, since the intention is to speak of direct visibility, primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the like are not included, as they are perceived only through the medium of the instruments of cognition. Alternatively, one might argue that what is enjoined by the scriptures and other authorities is that the Self's "visibility" consists solely in its being pervaded by a mental modification (*vṛtti*), and not in its being pervaded by the result in the form of illumination;
for the Self, whose very nature is self-luminous, lacks any dependence upon external illumination.

Therefore, in this context, "visibility" means "being made manifest," and since that does not exist in the self (*ātman*), that [position of yours] is also hollow. For just as you assert that the self— though experienced as "I"— is not pervaded by the fruit called consciousness (*caitanya*),
so too it is accepted by the Buddhists that the intellect (*buddhi*), even when possessing pleasure, pain, and so forth, is not pervaded by consciousness due to its own self-luminosity.

And thus, just as in the case of the self (*ātman*), because it is not established as an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*) even in the case of the intellect (*buddhi*), the discrimination of the intellect by way of its nature as an object of perception—though absolutely required—is not established; for this reason, various refutations have been stated in the *Bhāṣya* and elsewhere.
This is the general direction [of the argument].
Now, one might object: "In this way, the apprehension of discrimination in a general form is indeed possible."

Even so, there are indeed many universals—such as being transformable (*pariṇāmitva*), acting through combination (*saṃhatyakāritva*), consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion (*sukha-duḥkha-moha-ātmakatva*), and comprising the twenty-four principles (*caturviṃśati-tattvatva*)—and if liberation were caused by the discernment of these through their respective forms, one might object that there is the fault of lack of pervasion (*ananugama*). This is not so;
for there is pervasion precisely by way of [discernment] being knowledge that obstructs ego-inflation (*abhimāna-pratibandhaka-jñānatvena*).

Now, one might ask: "If it is the discrimination (*viveka*) in its general form alone that removes all forms of false identification (*abhimāna*), how can the specific forms of discriminative apprehension—such as 'I am not the body' and 'I am not the senses'—which are stated in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* to be the cause of liberation, be logically consistent? This is not so, because those intermediate forms of discrimination are merely an expansion (*prapañca*) of the general discrimination.

Thus ends the section on the nature of discriminative knowledge, which is the cause of liberation, in the *Sāṅkhyasāra* composed by the venerable Vijñānabhikṣu. Now begins the third chapter. Now, it is asked: "Who are these [principles] beginning with *prakṛti*, from which the *puruṣa* is to be distinguished? To this it is replied:
Primordial nature, intellect, ego, the five subtle elements, the eleven organs,
and the gross elements— these twenty-four are indeed common [to all].

Within these very categories, qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), and universals (*sāmānya*) are included by way of the non-difference between the property and the substratum (*dharmadharmyabheda*).

Among these, "primordial nature" (*prakṛti*) is the state of being the material cause of all transformations, whether directly or through a succession; this is based on the etymological derivation that its form (*ākṛti*) is "excellent" (*prakṛṣṭa*) in the sense of being a transformation.

Primordial nature, power (*śakti*), the unborn (*ajā*), the primary matter (*pradhāna*), the unmanifest (*avyakta*), darkness (*tamas*), illusion (*māyā*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and so forth, are synonyms for primordial nature.
The supreme sages declare that this [power] is called Brāhmī, as well as Vidyā, Avidyā, Māyā, Prakṛti, and Parā.
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti. And that [state] is the triad of substances, beginning with *sattva*, as characterized by the state of equilibrium.

The phrase "characterized" is included at the end to exclude the *sattva* and other qualities when they exist as effects. Furthermore, the state of equilibrium is a condition of non-combination due to the absence of deficiency or excess; that is to say, it is the non-causal state.
However, the effects beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), such as the sattva and other guṇas, never exist in a state that is not an effect; thus, there is an exclusion of that [state].
It was stated that they are "characterized" even in their state of disequilibrium in order to establish their status as primordial nature (prakṛti).
The term "non-effect," however, is the extracted meaning of the end of that characterization.
It should not be suspected that *prakṛti* possesses the qualities of *sattva* and so forth while being distinct from *sattva* and the rest;

for the *Sāṅkhyasūtra* states, "The non-qualification of *sattva* and the others by those [qualities] is because they are of the nature of those [qualities]," thereby denying that *sattva* and the others are attributes of *prakṛti* on the grounds that they constitute the very essence of *prakṛti*.
Furthermore, both the *Yogasūtra* and its commentary state that the *guṇas* themselves are *prakṛti*.
Furthermore, since the production of effects arises from the *guṇas* alone, the postulation of a primordial nature (*prakṛti*) distinct from them is redundant.
Statements such as "the *guṇas* are of the primordial nature" should be understood as being like the expression "the trees of the forest.
Thus: "Sattva, rajas, and tamas—the *guṇas* arose from the primordial nature."

Thus, the statement that *sattva* and the other qualities are effects of *prakṛti* refers only to the *sattva*, etc., which constitute the effects that serve as the causes of the principle of *mahat*, because it contradicts the scriptural statements regarding the permanence of the *guṇas*.
For the creation of *mahat* and the rest is heard [in scripture] to arise from the inequality (*vaiṣamya*) of the *guṇas*.

And that inequality is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) capable of being designated as *sattva*, etc., which is endowed with results such as illumination and is distinguished from other *guṇas* through its commingling with members of its own class.
By this, the position of twenty-eight principles (*tattva*) should also be understood as established.
Furthermore, the usage of the terms *sattva* and so forth is seen in the Śruti precisely in the context of their differentiation.

As it is said: "In the beginning, this was only darkness (*tamas*); impelled by that which is beyond it, it attains a state of inequality. This indeed is the form of *rajas*; impelled, it attains a state of inequality; this indeed is the form of *sattva*."
The triad beginning with *sattva*— namely *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*— is to be regarded as possessing qualities such as pleasure, illumination, lightness, and clarity,

as well as possessing conjunction, disjunction, and so forth, and as being non-dependent and serving as material causes; nevertheless, because they are instruments for the *puruṣa* and because they bind the *puruṣa*, they are designated by the term "guṇas," just like the sense organs and other faculties.

The doctrine that the *guṇas* consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion is due to the non-difference between a property and its possessor (*dharma* and *dharmin*), just as the mind is said to consist of volition (*saṅkalpa*).
In this regard, *sattva* possesses many properties such as pleasure, clarity, and illumination; however, it is primarily described as consisting of pleasure.
In this way, *rajas* also possesses many attributes, such as causing suffering, turbidity, and activity; however, it is said to be primarily of the nature of suffering (*duḥkha*).
Likewise, *tamas* also possesses many attributes, such as delusion, obscuration, and paralysis; however, it is said to be primarily of the nature of delusion (*moha*).
These very attributes constitute their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, the designations *sattva* and so forth are etymological.

For, according to the derivation "the state of being (*bhāva*) of that which exists (*sat*)"—meaning "existence" (*sattva*) as "supremacy"—the meaning of the word *sattva* is the supreme instrument for the person, characterized primarily by *dharma*.
And the meaning of the word *rajas* is the intermediate [quality], due to its association with passion (*rāga*).
And the meaning of the word "darkness" (tamas) is the lowest [quality], because it is conjoined with the obstruction of dharma. Furthermore,
those [qualities] such as sattva and the others each consist of innumerable individual manifestations.
"According to the Sāṅkhya Sūtra, 'The qualities (guṇas) possess mutual similarity and dissimilarity through properties such as lightness and so forth.

For in this sūtra, the similarity of many instances of *sattva* is established by means of lightness and so on, while its dissimilarity from *rajas* and *tamas* is established by those very same properties.
Likewise, the similarity and dissimilarity of many instances of *rajas* and many instances of *tamas* are stated respectively through mobility and so forth, and heaviness and so forth."
Furthermore, if the triad of sattva and the other two were each a single individual entity, then that triad would have to be described as omnipresent (*vibhu*),
since it is heard in scripture that there is at one time the creation of many brahmāṇḍas and so forth;
and if that were the case, the infinite variety of effects would not be possible.
Nor should it be argued that diversity [of experience] arises from the diversity of conjunctions;
for it is impossible for there to be diversity of conjunction among the three all-pervading qualities (guṇas) by themselves,
and because there exists no other substance to serve as a limiting factor.
Therefore, it is established that *sattva* and the other [guṇas] are indeed substances (*dravya*) consisting of innumerable individual instances.

Regarding them, the statement that there are three is like the Vaiśeṣikas' statement that there are nine substances, based on the three classifying attributes (*vibhājakopādhi*) such as *sattvatva* and so forth.
Furthermore, these *sattva* and the others possess atomic or all-pervading dimensions (*parimāṇa*) as appropriate.
Otherwise, it would contradict the statement that *rajas* has a mobile nature;
furthermore, it would be more appropriate for space to be the cause, as it possesses omnipresence (*vibhutva*).
Moreover, if all causal substances were omnipresent, it would be impossible for their effects to be limited in extent.
If it is argued that, in this way, the very atoms of earth and so forth as described by the Vaiśeṣikas constitute the primordial material cause (*prakṛti*), we say no;
for our position is distinct because the causal substances lack qualities such as odor, and thus the nature of earth (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth does not exist in them.
This has been stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa and other texts.
That which is the unmanifest cause is called Pradhāna by the best of sages;
it is the subtle Prakṛti, eternal, and consisting of both the existent and the non-existent.

Devoid of sound and touch, and unjoined with form and the other [sensory qualities], it consists of the three guṇas; it is the womb of the world, without beginning, and the source of both its origin and its dissolution.
By such statements as these, we have already refuted in our commentary the Vaiśeṣika inference of odor and other qualities within causal substances.

Now, if it is argued that even so, since primordial nature (*prakṛti*) consists of multiple manifestations such as *sattva* and the rest—which are common to both atoms and the omnipresent—this would undermine the established tenets of its being undivided, unitary, and inactive; do not say so.
This is because its being unlimited is stated precisely by virtue of its being the primordial material cause (*prakṛti*) in the form of the substance that is the cause;
just as odors, by virtue of being odors, pervade the earth.

Furthermore, it is because the established doctrine of the pervasiveness of the primordial material cause is justified precisely by the all-pervasiveness of the primordial causes such as space (*ākāśa*).
Likewise, because the meaning of the word "one" (eka) is precisely the absence of differentiation— whether by distinction of persons or by distinction of creations—
as is understood from the scripture stating, "the unborn, one" (ajāmekām); and furthermore,
because the meaning of the word "inactive" (akriya) is precisely the state of being devoid of activities such as determination and self-conceit.

Otherwise, the agitation of primordial nature (prakṛti) as described in the Śrutis and Smṛtis would be untenable; furthermore, other specific details concerning primordial nature are to be found in the Bhāṣya. And this is an inference of primordial nature.

The effects beginning with Mahat, which consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion, are the products of substances consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, because they themselves consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion, just like beds and other effects such as clothing.
Regarding this, scripture and tradition serve as supporting reasoning.
Thus, while Prakṛti is inferred in its general form, its specific characteristics are to be understood from the scriptures and through yoga.
Because inference has only the universal as its object.

[Objection: But pleasure and so forth are perceived only internally; what is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for pleasure and so forth in external objects, by virtue of which they could serve as an example?
It is said in reply:
Pleasure and so forth are established in relation to objects because the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is the cause of pleasure and so forth.
Nor is it the case that excellence and so forth residing in form and other qualities alone are the determinants for the production of pleasure and so forth;
for if excellence and so forth were of the nature of a universal (jāti), there would result a confusion of universals with blue-ness, yellow-ness, and the like.
Furthermore, because a single manifestation of form produces pleasure or pain depending on differences such as time and other factors,
being possessed of pleasure and so forth is itself what constitutes excellence and the like.

Moreover, just as there is the cognition "the color of a jar," from cognitions such as "the pleasure of a woman" or "the pleasure of sandalwood," it is appropriate that pleasure and the like reside in the object.
However, more [detail] is to be seen in the Bhāṣya.
Thus, primordial nature (prakṛti) has been defined;
now the principle of the Great One (mahattattva) is being defined.
From Prakṛti arises the principle called Mahat, known as the intellect (buddhi).
It receives the name "Mahat" due to its association with preeminent qualities such as dharma; that indeed is its defining characteristic.
Furthermore, "Mahān," "Buddhi," and "Prajñā" are its synonyms.
And so it is said in the Anugītā:
"The Great Self (Mahān Ātmā), Intellect (Mati), Viṣṇu, Jiṣṇu, and the heroic Śambhu;
likewise Intellect (Buddhi), Wisdom (Prajñā), Perception (Upalabdhi), as well as Brahmā, Fortitude (Dhṛti), and Memory (Smṛti)."
By these synonymous terms, the Great Self is described:
"He has hands and feet everywhere; He has eyes, heads, and faces everywhere."
Possessing ears everywhere in the world, he stands pervading all;
he is the power of atomization, levitation, attainment, and sovereignty—the imperishable light.
Furthermore, those who possess knowledge, who are free from greed, who have conquered their anger, and who are liberated—
all these indeed attain greatness.
Moreover, in the primordial creations, Viṣṇu himself becomes the self-existent Lord.

Thus [it is said]. Here, because the Great Principle (*mahat*) serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the three deities through its three constituents beginning with *sattva*, it is designated as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva due to the non-discrimination (*aviveka*) of those [deities] from it.
As it is stated regarding Viṣṇu: "The Great Principle is threefold: *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa*."
Thus it is said; and in the *Mātsya*:
"From the primary matter (pradhāna), together with its modifications, the principle of the Great One (mahattattva) was born;
for from that which is called 'the Great' (mahat), the manifestation (khyāti) of the worlds always arises."
From the qualities being agitated, three gods were born;
they are a single form, the three gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
Thus, the mention of the powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth is due to the non-difference between the attribute (*dharma*) and the possessor of the attribute (*dharmī*).

Even with respect to Brahmā and Śaṅkara, it is stated by the half-verse beginning with "Viṣṇu alone" that in the beginning, the Great Principle (*mahat-tattva*) manifests first specifically in the form of Viṣṇu.

That very same Great Principle, when transformed through a partial admixture of *rajas* and *tamas*, becomes the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for individual souls (*vyaṣṭi-jīva*); being joined with demerit (*adharma*) and other qualities, it also becomes limited.
According to the Sāṅkhya Sūtra, "the Great Principle (mahat) is the opposite of the supreme attachment" (*mahad-uparāgāt*).
The function (*vṛtti*) of the Great Principle is primarily and specifically determination (*adhyavasāya*).
The Great Principle is the seed-state of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which consists of the triad of the Great Principle, the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and the mind (*manas*).
In this regard, regarding the order of creation— namely, that from *prakṛti* comes the Great One (*mahat*), and from the Great One comes the Ego (*ahaṅkāra*)— the scripture alone is the authority.

For while through inference one may generally establish that effects possess causes, no inference capable of determining a specific sequence— whether the sequence of the elements and so forth, or the sequence of the internal organs and so forth— is possible within the process of creation, due to the absence of any clear indicative mark (*liṅga*).
We have already demonstrated in our commentary that there exists some sign, however slight, supported by Śruti and Smṛti for the sequence beginning with Mahat;
the principle of Mahat has been defined.
Now, Ahaṅkāra (the ego-principle) is being defined.
From the principle of Mahat, the ego (ahaṅkāra) arises,
like a branch from a sprout;
and because its function consists of self-conceit (abhimāna), it is designated as "ego."
It is like the perception of a potter;
that is its very characteristic.
And its synonyms are declared in the *Kūrma-purāṇa*.
Egoism (ahaṅkāra) and self-conceit (abhimāna) are traditionally known as the agent and the thinker;
it is also called the self (ātman), the manifest (prakula), and the living soul (jīva), from which all activities proceed.
Thus it is said. And that egoity (ahaṅkāra), being threefold, is the cause of three kinds of effects.
As it is stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"The Vaikārika, the Taijasa, and the Bhūtādi which is indeed Tāmasa."
This threefold ego-sense indeed arose from the Great One (mahat).
From the Taijasa ego arise the ten sense organs, and from the Vaikārika ego arise the ten deities; here, the eleventh, the mind, is of both natures by virtue of its own quality.

"The creation of the elements and the subtle elements (tanmātras) arose from Bhūtādi; thus were the creatures produced. Here, "Vaikārika" refers to the Sāttvika [aspect], and "Taijasa" refers to the Rājasa [aspect].
"By its own quality" means by way of excellence in the form of assistance to the functions of the sense organs.
"Consisting of both" means having the nature of both the organs of knowledge and the organs of action;
for it is established by such scriptural passages as "My mind was elsewhere, I did not hear," that the mind acts as a cooperative factor for both types of sense organs.
And there are eleven sense-deities:
the deities of the directions, Vāta, Arka, Pracetas, Aśvi, Vahni, Indra, Upendra, Mitra, and Candra.
Thus, the ego (ahaṅkāra) has been defined.
Now the sense organs and so forth are being defined.
From the ego, first the mind (manas) arises.
From attachment to sound, the ear is born for that person of purified self;
likewise, from attachment to form, the eye arises, and the nose from the desire to grasp odors.
This is because, in the *Mokṣadharma* and other texts, it is heard that the sense organs and so forth have as their effects the mental functions of passion and the like.
Consequently, from the *ahaṃkāra*, the ten sense organs and the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*) arise preceded by volition (*saṅkalpa*).
Furthermore, since there is no relationship of cause and effect between the sense organs and the subtle elements, there is no fixed order [between them].
In that regard, there is no intermediate causal relationship among the sense faculties (*indriya*), because there is a lack of evidence;
however, such a relationship does exist among the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
It is as follows:

From the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*), by the sequence to be described, arises the subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*), which possesses both the qualities of sound and touch; in this manner, through the successive increase of one quality at a time, the remaining three subtle elements arise from each preceding subtle element, because the *Pātañjala-bhāṣya* states that there is a successive increase of one quality for each of the subtle elements.
And from those five subtle elements, the five gross elements (*pañca-bhūtāni*) are born.

Regarding that, the sequence for the production of the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*) from the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and through them, the gross elements (*bhūtas*), is stated in the *Kūrma*, *Viṣṇu*, and other Purāṇas.
As it is said in the *Kūrma*:
"The source of the elements (*bhūtādi*), undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of sound (*śabdamātra*)."
Space is hollow; from it arises that which has the characteristic of sound.
But space, undergoing transformation, produced the mere quality of touch;
from that, wind arises, and touch is considered its specific attribute.
"In this sequence," etc.

Now, one might object: "In that case, since the four elements beginning with space (ākāśa) would also be primary causes (prakṛti) by virtue of initiating other principles (tattva), the established doctrine that they are exclusively modifications (vikṛti) would be undermined.
We reply: No, because the Purāṇas state that space and the others function as causes toward the subtle elements (tanmātra) such as touch only through the support of the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra).
Thus, the production of the twenty-three principles has been described.

Therein, excluding the five gross elements and including the *ahaṅkāra* within the intellect (*buddhi*), there arises what is known as the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), consisting of seventeen components; it serves as the locus for the manifestation of the Self, like fuel for fire.
And that [subtle body], having arisen at the beginning of creation, persists until the dissolution of nature (*prākṛtapralaya*).
By means of that very [subtle body], the transmigration of living beings occurs between this world and the next.
Furthermore, since *prāṇa* is merely a specific modification (*vṛttibheda*) of the intellect (*buddhi*), it is not mentioned separately from the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*).
The basis of that subtle body consists of the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), because, like a painting, it cannot travel to another world without a support, being of such extreme subtlety.
And this subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) arises at the beginning as a single entity, serving as the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the Self-existent (svayambhū),
just like the gross body (sthūlaśarīra) called Virāṭ which is to be described later.

Thereafter, the individual subtle bodies (vyaṣṭiliṅgaśarīras), which serve as the limiting adjuncts for the individual souls (vyaṣṭijīvas) and are constituent parts of that [original] body, are differentiated from it.
Just as the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) of a son arises from the subtle body of the father,
so it has been stated by the author of the Sūtras:
"The distinction between individual manifestations is due to the particularity of karma."
Manu has also said:
"Having combined the subtle constituent parts of those six [elements] of immeasurable power with portions of his own self, he fashioned all beings."

Thus, the term "of the six" refers to the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*), which serve as an indicator for the entire subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*). Accordingly, the meaning is that the Self-existent One (*svayambhū*) created all living beings by joining the subtle and minute parts of his own subtle body to the portions of the self (*ātman*) within their respective conscious [faculties]. The subtle body has thus been defined.

The production of the gross body is now described: within the mahat-tattva increased tenfold is the ahaṃkāra; within the ahaṃkāra increased tenfold is space (vyoman); within space increased tenfold is air (vāyu); and within air increased tenfold is fire (tejas). Within fire increased tenfold... [is water]. Within water increased tenfold is earth. Within earth increased tenfold is the subtle body (liṅga-śarīra). Within the subtle body increased tenfold is the gross body (sthūla-śarīra). Thus, the gross body is produced from the subtle elements. Therefore, it is said that the gross body is composed of the five gross elements. Because it is composed of the five gross elements, it is called "gross" (sthūla).
