In the midst of water, and within ten times that amount of water, the earth arises;
this very [earth] is the seed of the gross body.
And that same seed, in the form of earth, transforms into the form of the embryo (bījamaṇḍa).
In the midst of that earth-envelopment, which is tenfold in size and has the form of an egg, there arises from his mere volition the gross body of Svayambhū, consisting of the fourteen worlds.
By means of that very body, Svayambhū is called Nārāyaṇa.
This was stated by Manu with reference to Svayambhū:
Desiring to emit various kinds of creatures, he, having meditated, first emitted water from his own body; into that water, he cast the seed.
Then that golden egg came into being, radiant as the thousand-rayed sun;
within it was born Brahmā himself, the grandfather of all the worlds.
He is indeed the first embodied being; he is called the Puruṣa. He is the original creator of all beings, and as Brahmā, he existed at the beginning.
The waters are called *nārāḥ*, for the waters are indeed the offspring of *nara*;
since they were his primordial abode (*ayana*), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa.

By the phrase "and so forth," [it is meant that] because the individual persons (vyaṣṭipuruṣa) originate from that very First Person and are dissolved back into Him at the end, He alone is designated as the one Self (ātman) in both Śruti and Smṛti. Therefore,
since this is intended for conventional usage, there is no contradiction with Śruti and Smṛti in the statement that Nārāyaṇa alone is the Self of all beings.

Then that Nārāyaṇa, the Virāṭ possessing a body, having created the Self-born one (Svayambhū) known as the Four-faced (Caturmukha) upon Sumeru— which serves as the pericarp of the lotus of his own navel— emitted through him all other individual embodied beings down to the level of stationary things.
And so it is recorded in the Smṛti:
From the limbs of that wise being, the knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas) were born together with those effects and instruments produced from his body.

Thus it is said. As for the scriptural account of the manifestation of the four-faced Brahmā from the navel-lotus, ears, eyes, and other organs of Nārāyaṇa reclining upon Śeṣa, that should be understood as occurring only during the daily creations according to the distinctions of the respective *kalpas*.

For it is only during the daily dissolutions (*dainandinapralaya*)—when the gods have entered and become one with the body of Nārāyaṇa and are asleep—that their manifestation in the sequence beginning with the four-faced one from the presence of Him who reclines upon Śeṣa is logical; it does not apply to the original creations (*ādisarga*), because [Nārāyaṇa] reclines in his playful form (*līlāvigraha*) only during the daily dissolutions.
Thus, in brief, the twenty-four principles (*tattvas*) have been stated, along with their purpose in the form of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*).
In this regard, whatever principle is born from something else, its stability consists precisely in being filled by that [source], and its dissolution also occurs therein.
Whatever principle is born from something, it dissolves back into that very place.
They dissolve in reverse order and are born in successive order.
Thus, from the *Bhārata* and other sources:
these gross transformations of the twenty-four principles, consisting of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, have been demonstrated for the sake of discriminating them from the immutable Puruṣa.
Other subtle transformations, occurring at every moment, are also recorded in the Smṛtis regarding them. Thus:
For the constituent parts are constantly appearing and disappearing;
because they occur with an imperceptible velocity over time and due to their subtlety, they are not seen.
Thus it is said. Therefore, every insentient object is declared to be, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), always non-existent.
Consequently, those who fear suffering should see that the Self alone is the ultimately real and should become detached from that [insentient world].
As it has been stated in the *Anugītā*:
The great tree has its origin in the seed of the Unmanifest;
it consists of the trunk of the intellect, has the great ego as its branches, and the sense organs as the hollows of its sprouts.
It has the great elements as its main branches and the specific qualities as its sub-branches;
it is ever-leaved and ever-flowering, yielding the fruit of both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
The eternal livelihood of all beings is the conduct of Brahman;
having understood this in its true essence through supreme knowledge as a sword, [one is liberated].
"Having cut [the bonds] and attained the state of the Imperishable, one abandons birth and death.
Thus ends the section on the determination of the nature of Prakṛti and the other factors that are the objects of discrimination, in the *Sāṅkhyasāra* composed by the venerable Vijñānabhikṣu.
Thus ends the first part of the *Sāṅkhyasāra*.
Now begins the second part.
The First Chapter.
Now, for the sake of easy comprehension by the disciples, the self (ātman) worthy of discernment, designated as the "Person" (puruṣa), is described by means of a series of verses. ViSs_2,1.1 //

In that regard, since the existence of the knower is established in a general sense by the force of the cognition "I know," he is therefore proven to possess attributes such as eternality and omnipresence.
The enjoyer is eternal, because all transformations beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) are for his sake and are produced by his karma, without distinction.

Moreover, because it serves as the substrate for the accumulation of unseen impressions (adṛṣṭa-saṃskāra) and exists in the form of a seed, the intellect (dhī) is beginningless; consequently, the beginninglessness of the enjoyer (bhoktṛ) is established.
Apart from the beginninglessness of the relationship between property and its owner, there can be no established status of an enjoyer;
however, ownership with respect to the intellects consists in possessing the impressions of the activities of one's own objects of enjoyment.
Ownership belongs to the experiencer because it consists in the activity of the impressions residing within oneself;
therefore, upon the destruction of ownership, the absolute liberation of the self is established.
Since there is no possible cause for the destruction of the enjoyer, who is a beginningless entity, the enjoyer does not undergo destruction; thus, the enjoyer is established as eternal.
The illumination of knowledge is produced for this [self]; however, it is not tenable if it were eternal, for the arising of illumination is never observed anywhere in that which is already luminous.
For in the effect known as light, that quality [of luminosity] belongs to its constituent parts;
therefore, light is not impermanent in an eternal substance.

Due to the conjunction of light and its substrate, there is the delusion of the production of light in fuel where light already abounds, and in a mirror due to the removal of an obstruction. ViSs_2.1.10 //
Therefore, if the knowledge of an eternal self were to be eternal,
then, for the sake of parsimony, it is more reasonable to postulate that knowledge itself is the self, existing without a substratum.
Because it is independent, that [self] is considered a substance, as are conjunction and so forth;
therefore, the cognition "I" and so on is also logically established in relation to consciousness.
For the ignorant, the notion of a "lump" regarding a physical aggregate is indeed certain due to beginningless defects;
however, the cognition that perceives the nature of knowledge within that same aggregate is valid.
Or let there be cognitions of being supported, smallness, birth, destruction, and so forth,
just as in the case of the auditory organ [cognizing] space, regarding the cognition of an object as mere cognition itself.
Therefore, by means of parsimonious reasoning, due to the absence of sublation,
and through scripture and other authorities, the eternal self is established as being of the very nature of consciousness.
That knowledge is all-pervading because of its eternity and also because it pervades the body;
for if it were of medium size, it would be subject to destruction, and if it were atomic, it would occupy only a small space.
Even though there is sovereign power, because there is direct observation only of the fluctuations of one's own intellect,
it does not follow that everything is perceived everywhere and at all times within cognition.
The appearance of an object within the mind is considered by the wise to be a reflection of that object;
for it is only the mental activity (*vṛtti*) that possesses the capacity for direct reflection within the mind (*citi*).
Therefore, even though the all-pervading, eternal, and immutable consciousness is unattached,
the manifestation of other objects is held— on the strength of the resulting experience— to occur solely through the medium of its mental modifications (vṛtti).

Through positive and negative concomitance, because they are produced by mental modifications (vṛtti), all [afflictions] such as desire reside in cognitions alone, sharing the same locus as the modification, and not in the self. (ViSs 2.1.20)
Therefore, because all internal modifications abide within their respective cognitions,
the entire multitude of the space of consciousness remains uniform and eternally immutable.
Eternally pure, eternally awakened, eternally liberated, and stainless;
self-luminous and without support, it is like a lamp among all things.
"Surely, let there be only one self for all, due to parsimony, just as it is with space;
[and let] pleasure, pain, and so forth reside in the cognitions alone, because they are distinct [from the self]. If this is argued, it is not so. (ViSs 2.1.23)

Even though the collection of conscious entities (cidgaṇa) is uniform in nature, mutual differentiation among them is established by the Śruti and Smṛti through their distinct characteristics, such as the possession or non-possession of enjoyments.
Even its experience (*bhoga*), which consists of the reflection of pleasure and so forth, does not exist in reality;
nevertheless, existence and non-existence within its consciousness (*cit*) would indeed serve as its differentiators.

Just as the dark and red colors, which are adventitious, differentiate a crystal, your own example is dissimilar because the property of difference is not established in the case of space. (ViSs 2.1.26)
Thus ends the section on the Nature of the Puruṣa in the *Sāṅkhyasāra* composed by the venerable Vijñānabhikṣu.
Now begins the second chapter.

Now, I shall explain in detail the distinction between the Self and the non-Self, which consists of their respective qualities and defects, so that their discrimination may become perfectly clear. (ViSs 2.2.1)
In the space of the mass of the universal self, this cloud of the world is born and dissolves again and again, its powers being stirred by proximity.

Therefore, consciousness (citi) is the material cause of the universe by way of being its substratum, through the transformations of the powers consisting of the three guṇas, while remaining itself changeless.

Just as water is considered the material cause of the earth by way of its subsistence within it, so too is consciousness held to be the material cause of the earth through the medium of the subtle element (tanmātra) of earth in its natural state.
Therefore, although Brahman is the material cause of the world, because it is devoid of modification,
it is called the "unchanging," the "eternal," the "synonym for the ultimate reality," and the "ultimately real."
Because it serves its own purpose and because it is established through one's own experience, it is ultimately real;
for by its own persistence and its own establishment, it is indeed regarded as "existent" by the world.
Due to their disappearance through various forms that undergo change at every moment,
all insentient objects— from primordial matter (*prakṛti*) onwards— are unreal, like waves in the ocean.
"That which does not acquire another designation even after the lapse of time—
such as those arising from transformation and so forth— is a real entity," according to such traditional teachings.
Because its existence is dependent upon another, and because it is established through the perspective of another,
it is considered to exist or not exist only in relation to that other.
"But the existence of that which exists is not non-existence; how could there be reality in non-existence?
Thus, according to the *Gāruḍa*, the distinction between existence and non-existence is established.
Therefore, this world is neither existent nor non-existent, but consists of both existence and non-existence;
and because its object is non-existent, that cognition is an ontological error.
Consciousness is the essence of the world-tree, while everything else is without essence; for within the phenomenal world, consciousness alone is the stable portion, owing to its changelessness.
Everything other than that is declared to be void because it lacks essence;
likewise, it is unreal and non-existent as well, due to its instability relative to that [reality].
Such is the nature of the existence of the self and the non-existence of others as shown in the *Vāsiṣṭha* and other works; it is stated here in brief, though it is explained at length therein.
In the waking state, the dream is unreal; in the dream, the waking state is unreal.
Death is unreal in birth, and in death, birth too is composed of unreality.
The delusion that consists of the world is never non-existent, nor does it ever exist as something real; it remains like a bubble on the water.
The Self alone is the supreme reality; other perceptions of worldly existence are not so, just like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell or a mirage in the desert.
There exists the all-pervading, tranquil, pure, and solid mass of the Supreme Self;
it is the vast, supreme space, whose body is inconceivable pure consciousness alone.
That is all-pervading, possessed of all powers, everything itself, and the self of all;
wherever and in whatever manner it arises, and however it abides, it is indeed exactly so in each case.
In that which is infinitely vast, the waves of the three worlds— consisting of manifestation and disappearance—
quiver like mirages in a desert.
Just as a river of water exists while its waves are moving,
so the splendor of the world is extended by the mind alone, like a magical illusion.
The entire universe is stretched out by the self-existent Brahmā through the mind alone;
therefore, this universe which is perceived is composed of mind.
For that person of impure intellect who is deluded and not established in the expansive state,
this world— which is like the essence of a diamond— exists as if it were real, though it is actually unreal.
Just as for one who lacks analytical discernment, there may be the cognition of a bracelet in gold or brass,
yet there is not even the slightest notion of "gold" [in the case of brass].

Likewise, for the ignorant person, there exists only this perception of the visible world, resplendent with oceans, houses, mountains, and great serpents; there is no other perception of ultimate reality.
By such statements in the Vāsiṣṭha, the absolute unreality of the world is not asserted;
for by other passages, the world is considered to be a real effect produced from primordial matter (prakṛti).
Some call that in which the world abides, being entirely free from name and form, "Prakṛti"; others call it "Māyā," and still others "atoms. (ViSs 2.27)
Just as the lines of a lotus-wheel exist within a stone during the state of deep sleep, so too does this series of worlds reside within consciousness.

Because of the description of the Sāṅkhya doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) and other tenets in such statements as: "The creeper of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) has grown in the sky, bearing the great fruit of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). (ViSs 2.29)
Thus ends the section on the distinction between the reality of the Self and the unreality of the non-Self, in the *Sāṅkhyasāra* composed by the venerable Vijñānabhikṣu.
Now begins the third section.
Thus, the existence of the Self has been shown as distinct from others;
now I shall describe its nature as consciousness, which is distinct from the fluctuations of the intellect.
Experience, consciousness, awareness, and sensation are said to be the Spirit (puruṣa);
the knowable, which is insentient, dark, and ignorance, is called Primordial Matter (pradhāna) and so forth. (ViS 2.3.2)
Feeling is designated as the "feeler" precisely because of its connection with the object to be felt,
just as light is called the "illuminator" because of its connection with the object to be illuminated.
Or, just as the manifestation of an object through its coloring by the object itself is the illuminator of that object,
so too the part consisting of the self, colored by the cognized, serves as the substratum for the possessor of parts.
In the unattached consciousness, this coloring by the object of knowledge does not occur as it does in the cognitions;
rather, it is the reflection of that [object] in consciousness, either directly or through a medium.
Due to the absence of the instrument called the external function, consciousness—though all-pervasive—is not at all colored by it; thus, it does not perceive the object of cognition anywhere.
Likewise, consciousness (cit), due to the absence of an instrument called a mental modification (vṛtti),
remains as an unknown reality in the absence of a modification directed toward itself.
Thus, consciousness is formless, having the nature of luminous space;
it remains in an unmanifest state during liberation and similar states due to the absence of mental activity.
The modification of the intellect (buddhi-vṛtti), however, possesses form and is delimited like a lamp;
it is always manifest, likewise innumerable, and momentary.
And because it is perceived by another, the mental modification (vṛtti) is considered to be insentient, like a jar or a lamp;
however, its luminosity is indeed nothing other than the sense organ itself, due to its taking on the form of the object.
Just as a mirror is the illuminator of that [face] because it possesses its form,
so too is that very [emptiness] the illuminator of all things because it is capable of assuming all forms.
Furthermore, the capacity to see does not belong to consciousness as something distinct from its modification;
for if both were postulated as knowers, there would be the fault of unnecessary complexity (gaurava).
But another object mounted upon the intellect and reflected therein by means of that [intellect], experience perceives; no other seer exists, such as the intellect or anything else whatsoever.

Thus, the distinctness of consciousness from the modifications of the intellect has been declared; this difference, known as the distinction between the conscious and the unconscious, is even more evident when compared to the body and its like.

Due to the similarity arising from mutual reflection between the modification and consciousness, there is the conventional usage of "consciousness" with respect to the modification, just as there is the conventional usage of "fire" with respect to iron [in contact with fire]. (ViSs 2.3.15)
This discrimination between the activity and the consciousness cannot be accomplished by one of meager intellect;
for it is here that logicians are utterly deluded, which is why the Sāṅkhyas possess preeminence.
Due to the failure to distinguish between the mental mode and its cognition, the Buddhist Vijñānavādins,
being deluded regarding the scriptural teaching on the known nature of the Self, conceived of consciousness as momentary.
This distinction between the sentient being and the person, and between the form of the mental state and its cognition,
cannot be made by the wise, just as it is impossible for swans to separate milk from water.
This is the limit of saṃsāra, and liberation is established right there; it is the ascertainment of that awakening through discernment from its various mental modifications. (ViS 2.3.19)
Everyone experiences experience, yet no one experiences its state as being experienced;
for when it is manifesting, one requires only the act of discrimination regarding it.
The self cannot be distinguished from external objects because of the intermingling of its functions;
therefore, it must be distinguished within its own function by means of the awareness of that very function.
Just as fire mixed with embers cannot be distinguished by the intellect, yet that same fire is clearly distinguishable from the embers by its quality of burning wood; so too is the Self.
Therefore, in the Śruti, by means of distinguishing the activity of the objects seen in a dream,
the witness of that [activity] is shown to be of the nature of self-luminous consciousness.
That which is directly manifest as something is considered by the wise to be distinct from it, just as light is distinct from jars and the like, and mental modifications are distinct from light.
Because the self is directly manifest, it is of the nature of experience;
therefore, the self is distinct from the mental modifications—this is the swift path in one's own philosophical system.
In this and other such ways, because it is distinct from the illumination of the *buddhi-sattva*,
the consciousness-illumination (*cit-prakāśa*) is established as its illuminator.
Therefore, by means of the examples of the dream-body and so forth shown in the Śruti and other scriptures,
consciousness is considered to be distinct from the waking body, senses, and objects.
In a dream, the body and all else appear within consciousness as non-different from consciousness;
in the waking state it is the same, with this distinction only: that even the external appears.
Because it consists of mind, everything in a dream is directly an object of consciousness;
whereas in the waking state, the external world becomes the range of consciousness through the medium of the sense organs.

The entire body and so forth appear with the same form in both dream and waking within the space of consciousness; herein, there is no distinction based on the difference between external objects and internal states.
In the sky of consciousness, the intellect takes on the form of objects either through latent impressions or through valid means of knowledge;
therefore, the manifestation of objects to consciousness is the same in both dreaming and waking states.
This very point is stated through one's own direct experience and not from hearsay;
there is no means for the vision of the Self other than that which is like the analogy of a dream. (ViSs 2.3.32)
For just as in deep sleep one perceives everything within one's own self as if in a dream,
so too in the waking state one regards the Self as being situated in a single location.
Deep sleep is the true nature of the self, because it is then established in its own essential form;
whereas waking and dreaming are illusory, for the intellect perceives them as having a false semblance of reality.

The deep sleep of the intellect is an obscuration by tamas; the deep sleep of consciousness is the opposite of that—the state of being devoid of the obscuration of the perceivable known as mental modification (vṛtti). (ViS 2.3.35)
Full, immutable, and eternal, the Person perceives only the activity of his own respective intellect; because of the absence of any visible object called "activity," he never perceives anything else.
Just as there is awareness in the place where the function [of the senses] occurs, so it is everywhere and at all times;
yet the deluded suffer in vain for themselves through the loss of wealth and other such things. (ViSs 2.3.37)
The wife of the body is the primary cause of the great disease of experiencing suffering;
yet fools do not abandon her, because they find pleasure in the sleep of ignorance.
If one does not abandon the household life of beginningless ignorance through discernment, there is no liberation; external renunciation yields at best only happiness in this world and the next.
Since one's own self and the selves of others are always of the nature of pure consciousness alone,
the distinction between "self" and "other" is false, being merely a conceptual construction of the intellect.
Having superposed the agency of the self upon the Lord, who is pure consciousness and devoid of qualities,
the intellect is bound by its own actions through the offense of disregarding the Lord.
But a virtuous wife, seeing her husband according to his true nature and being devoted to him,
becomes filled with bliss in this world and, at the end, shall attain dissolution within the body of her husband.
"I am not the doer, nor am I happy or miserable; I am of the nature of the space of pure consciousness.
Thinking thus of the Lord, she did not cause her husband to experience suffering.
Thus ends the chapter on the distinction between the sentience of the Self and the insentience of the non-Self, in the *Sāṅkhyasāra* composed by the venerable Vijñānabhikṣu.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Thus has the self been described as distinct from the intellect and other faculties;
now its nature as consciousness and likewise its nature as bliss will be explained.
"Suffering is the longing for sensual pleasure; happiness is the transcendence of both suffering and pleasure.
From this traditional teaching, it follows that the nature of happiness belongs to the self, which is eternally free from suffering.
It is universally accepted that the conventional meaning is set aside by the force of a technical definition;
otherwise, this definition would be rendered useless in the scripture of liberation.

Alternatively, by means of indirect speech (*parokṣavāda*), for the sake of attaining supreme endearment, pleasant discourse regarding her form is used toward a man, just as one uses the word "self" (*ātman*) to attain mastery over it. (ViSs 2.4.4)
This is clear from such scriptural passages as "neither bliss nor devoid of bliss," which,
when combined with logical reasoning, negate the nature of bliss in the Self.

Because it is devoid of any object to be approached, and because of the scriptural statement "not this, not this," the prohibitive statement is stronger than an injunctive statement; such is the established rule.

And the term "devoid of bliss" expresses the state of being an enjoyer of the bliss of one's own adjuncts, which consists in the nature of ownership; for it is just as when one says "not poor," [implying the possession of wealth]. ViSs_2.4.7 //
The Self is declared to be dearer than everything else, even than pleasure, by the Śruti;
therefore, it is not appropriate to describe that Self as being pleasure itself.
According to the Vedānta Sūtra, "Bliss and so forth belong to the Pradhāna";
thus, even in the Vedānta, it is not established that the Self is of the nature of bliss.
The fact that consciousness is not of the nature of happiness has been examined by us at length in the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya*; now, love (*preman*) is being explained.
The metaphorical expression "May we not cease to exist; may I always exist" refers to that supreme love which is an attachment to consciousness (*cit*) without any external cause. (ViS 2.4.11)
This attachment of the intellect, being directed toward nothing else, does not exist even toward pleasures;
therefore, one's own self is most dear, and nothing else is more dear than it. (ViSs 2.4.12)
Love for the self as the self does not depend on its being pleasant or anything else; for while one might wish "May I exist," one does not wish "May I be happy. (ViSs 2.4.13)
And likewise, neither happiness nor the absence of suffering, nor even selfhood, is established as the cause for affection; rather, it is self-love itself that is the cause. (ViS 2.4.14)
Therefore, in reality, the self alone is dear, because all other things are merely adventitious;
the affection for anything else is adventitious and, due to its instability, is not ultimate.
Elsewhere, pleasure regarding objects such as happiness arises from the non-discrimination of impermanence and so forth;
however, the soul's own pleasure is eternal, and therefore the person is considered to be eternally blissful.
If the concentrated mind perceives that its own state of being dear is superior to all else,
why then does it not sink into the ocean of bliss?
Since happiness is seen in the worlds through the pleasant appearance of the Buddha,
one may infer from this that supreme happiness arises from the sight of the supremely beloved.
"Because it serves the self's own purpose, there is affection everywhere; the self is dear by its very nature.
Thus the Śruti constantly declares this, with the desire to bring about the vision of the Self.
Even beyond that, the incomparable happiness derived from beholding one's own beloved Self should be known;
the steadfast ones of great intelligence, liberated while living, enjoy that bliss.
Not seeing the truth of inner self-bliss, which is non-deceptive for the yogi, the wretched person seeking external pleasure is deceived. (ViSs 2.4.21)
The embodied soul, looking outward with a desire for pleasure through the apertures of the senses, perceives happiness within by means of the windows; it does not perceive that which is external.

Fie upon those semblances of pleasure arising from sense objects—attained with difficulty, consisting of suffering, resulting in extreme pain in their transformation, and obstructing one's own true happiness! (ViSs 2.4.23)
Thus ends the chapter on the distinction between the nature of pleasure and pain in the Self and the non-Self, composed by the venerable Vijñānabhikṣu in the *Sāṅkhyasāra*.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
That which consists of the nature of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss has been described in three chapters.
The three characteristics of the Self, as proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti, [are as follows]: // ViSs_2,5.1 //
The opposite of these is clearly described as the characteristic of others;
however, the discernment between these two—virtue and fault—is the supreme remover of defects.

Hereafter, I shall briefly state many other points of dissimilarity between the person (puruṣa) and primordial nature (prakṛti), such as their being devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) and possessing qualities (saguṇa), respectively. 2.5.3.
Because pleasure and the like are produced by a mental state (*dhi*) functioning in the form of an object,
they are postulated as being in a relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with cognitions for the sake of parsimony.
Since the Great One (mahat) and the rest are insentient, their cause is also held to be insentient;
for in the world, a similarity of nature between cause and effect is observed everywhere.
Therefore, by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), the Self is established as pure consciousness alone;
all qualities such as *prakṛti* and the rest, as well as all other transformations, are merely its modifications.
Likewise, the Self is considered by the wise to be devoid of qualities and immutably fixed;
the designation "immutably fixed" (kūṭastha) is applied to consciousness because of its stability, like the peak of a mountain.
If there is a connection with another, it is colored by that form;
just as a latent impression (vāsanā) arises in the intellect due to its connection with an object. (ViSs 2.5.8)
From the contact of substances with a vessel or other such object, there arises the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of each respective substance;
the cause of this coating is the connection (*sambandha*), while attachment (*saṅga*) is that which is connected, namely the ointment (*añjana*).
Therefore, the Supreme Seers describe the Person as stainless, unattached, and untainted, using such analogies as the sky and the lotus leaf.
In the infinite ocean of the power of pure consciousness, the powers of *sattva* and the other *guṇas*, impelled by the winds of human goals,
assume the form of the bubbles of the universe.
Therefore, the Lord is indeed the conscious self who, through mere proximity, acts as the impeller of the insentient world—like a magnet for iron or like a jewel [for its rays]. (ViS 2.5.12)
The Person alone is the creator of the world, the sustainer of the world, and the Lord of all; for the insentient multitude proceeds toward its master just as servants do for their lord. (ViS 2.5.13)
And the instruments within bodies, like officials for the sake of a king,
naturally present the various objects of experience to the minister of the mind.
The intellect makes itself known to consciousness as being joined with those objects of enjoyment; the Self, the lord of all, enjoys them by mere observation, like a king. (ViS 2.5.15)
The body is the master of wealth and the like; the sense organs are the masters of the body;
the intellect is the mistress of the sense organs; and the Self is the supreme master of the intellect.
Since there is no other impeller for the immutable Lord,
the Seer, as the ultimate limit of the Lord, is indeed the Supreme Lord.
The sovereignty of another is crowded with many activities and is adventitious;
the sovereignty of the Self is effortless, faultless, and beginningless.
For the Self consists of all powers and performs the cosmic dance of the circle of powers; by means of Māyā, it effortlessly undergoes both saṃsāra and its cessation.
For the yogi who beholds this sovereignty of the Self— which surpasses all and is free from defect— even the sovereignty of Brahmā seems like a blade of grass.
The body is said to be the self of the external; the senses are the self of the body;
the intellect is the self of that which ends with the senses; but the sky of consciousness is the self of the intellect.
Therefore, consciousness (citi) is called the Supreme Self (paramātman) by virtue of being the ultimate limit;
likewise, consciousness is called the individual soul (jīva) due to its association with the internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa).
And there is the traditional teaching that the Supreme Self is devoid of the effects of ignorance.
Whatever pervades something else, that is Brahman; therefore, earth and the other elements are [Brahman]. (Viśiṣṭādvaitasiddhāntasaṅgraha 2.5.23)

In the theistic Sāṅkhya doctrine as well, Brahman is held to extend up to primordial matter (prakṛti), depending on its respective effects; yet it is consciousness alone that is ultimately accepted [as the ultimate reality].
Others [claim] that the state of being the supreme self (paramātmatva) and so forth does not reside anywhere in the insentient;
for the Supreme Brahman is indeed sentient, due to its perceptibility and its pervasiveness.
For its presiding principle is all-pervasive, yet it does not exist as a cause;
indeed, it is an infinite self, a mass of space, undivided and of a single nature.
Therefore, he is designated as the mass of consciousness, the mass of cognition, and the mass of the Self;
for he is independent of any external light and is also the seer of himself.
The Self is said to be self-luminous, while others are of a different nature from it.
Enjoyment is consumption, and that does not exist in the immutable [Self] as it does in the intellects.
The state of being an enjoyer is secondary, consisting of the enjoyment of the reflection [of objects] within the fluctuations of the intellect;
however, because he directly perceives the fluctuations of the intellect, the Person is called the witness of the intellect. (ViSs 2.5.29)
Because he perceives all without undergoing modification, he is called the Witness of everything;
yet the witnesshood of consciousness is also non-permanent, since it consists in the coloring by the object of thought.
This [definition] is merely an illustration for the purpose of distinguishing [the self] from the insentient;
therefore, the person (puruṣa) is said to be indefinable, atomic (aṇu), and subtle (sūkṣma).
Because it is invisible apart from the visible, the existent is called unmanifest;
just as the invisible Rāhu is seen when he has seized the moon.
Just as the invisible face is seen in a mirror, so too is consciousness perceived within its own respective intellects.
If there were attachment of the universe to consciousness, the universe would appear at all times.
Therefore, although it is the support of all, consciousness is sung of as being empty like space;
for, due to the defects of the visible world, a false notion is superimposed upon that which is stainless by the act of seeing.
One suffers through the perception of defects in the mirror-like consciousness, as if it were a sky stained with impurity;
yet in reality, there is never any stain residing in the object of perception within consciousness.
And for this reason, the person is said to be stainless, established in its own nature, and faultless,
since there is no distinction characterized by heterogeneity among those of the same kind.
Therefore, the Self is declared to be equal because it is always of a single nature;
yet, by presiding over the body and through its manifestation in the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), the Person is called the embodied one (dehī). 2.5.37.
He is called "alone" because he is without a second and is solitary;
moreover, that Person is said to be "uncovered" due to the absence of obstruction to his power of consciousness.
And because he is the sovereign of all, the Self is the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) due to its knowledge of the field;
it sports playfully amidst the movements within the lotus-petal of the intellect situated in the lake of the heart.
Moving as it were among the fish of bliss, while consuming [them], it is called the *haṃsa*;
with the letter *ha* it goes outward, and with the letter *sa* it enters again.
By means of this vital function (prāṇavṛtti), the Self is called "Haṃsa";
it breathes within the cave of the heart inside the body, together with the wife that is the intellect (buddhi).
Being manifested together with her, as if sleeping within a cave,
he brings about the transformation of his own Māyā— which consists of the three qualities— through his mere presence.
The Self is called "the illusory one" (māyī) because it assumes the unreal disguises created by that [illusion];
its own eleven elements and these five [gross elements] make sixteen.
In reality, the parts of the Person do not exist; therefore, He is partless (niṣkala).
The word "I" denotes the master, and the master is indeed the witness of the mind. (ViSs 2.5.44)
Therefore, by the word "I," the wise declare pure consciousness alone—the Supreme Lord of all, the knower of all, the doer of all, the non-dual Person. (ViSs 2.5.45)
Just as one speaks of "the king" because he is the lord of all men due to his commonality [with others],
so too is there a description based on mere birth through the aphorism of the non-duality of the Self.
For at the time of dissolution, the selves are devoid of duality with anything of a different nature;
because they are unattached, they are eternally pure, and because they possess consciousness, they are eternally awakened.

"Likewise, the person (puruṣa) is considered eternally liberated because of his eternal freedom from suffering"—according to this direction taught in the scriptures of the Guru and through one's own direct experience. (ViSs 2.5.48)

Let the wise perform the discrimination of the Self from the non-Self through the fourfold discernment, based on the detailed distinction between the Person (puruṣa) and Primordial Matter (prakṛti). This collection of dissimilarities, when fully explained, grants swift liberation to those who meditate. 2.5.49.
Thus ends the chapter on the Attributes Contradictory to the Self in the *Sāṅkhyasāra* composed by the venerable Vijñānabhikṣu.
Now begins the sixth chapter:
Having understood discriminative discernment (*viveka*) itself through sound reasoning, it is then experienced.
How one should perform the royal yoga (rājayoga) is now stated in brief.
One who is incapable of Rājayoga possesses the qualification for Haṭhayoga;
this was stated by Bhusuṇḍa to Vasiṣṭha in the Vāsiṣṭha [Rāmāyaṇa]. (ViSs 2.6.2)
In Rājayoga, which is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind, and in Haṭha, which consists of breath control and postures, these two are primary;
yet they should be practiced as auxiliaries to one another according to one's capacity.
Those infinite defects in sense objects that have been proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti should first be scrutinized by yogis for the sake of stabilizing the mind.
Since infinite seeds of desire sprout within the heart,
the crop of wisdom and merit does not grow there, which resembles a wilderness.

When the seed of desire in the mind has been scorched by the fire of the vision of faults and the field of the mind has been plowed by the plows of the teacher and the scriptures, it flourishes in that excellent field.

Seeing the abundance of non-existence within what is considered real, the lack of beauty in what is beautiful, and the preponderance of suffering within pleasures, the wise person becomes dispassionate.
Even the world of Brahmā is a hell, filled with destruction and impurity;
it is joined by others who are superior to oneself, and it is also fraught with suffering due to the three qualities (guṇas).
Even those dwelling there strive for liberation, being fearful of rebirth;
therefore, it should be understood in brief that the entire world is joined with suffering.
"The mind is afflicted by desire, thinking 'may this be mine' and 'may this not be mine';
therefore, one should understand that the union of the mind with its own nature is suffering. (ViSs 2.6.10)
Deep sleep is supreme happiness; the perception of sense objects is suffering.
This is the sum total of happiness and suffering—what is the use of further prolixity?

Therefore, having examined objects that appear as either beneficial or harmful, the wise person who seeks the ultimate goal should abandon those things that are merely pleasing to the childish, just as one would avoid snakes.
Thus, by perceiving the endless faults [of passion] and through the discernment of its illusory nature, one should always contemplate the self as pure when passion has been attenuated. (ViSs 2.6.13)
Even by the Guru it cannot be pointed out as "this is that";
the reality of the Self of the indifferent one shines forth by itself.

"I am the essence of the awakening of the intellect, the witness of the intellect, the all-pervading one beyond the intellect, the immutable, the sun of consciousness"—thus one should contemplate with one-pointed concentration. (ViSs 2.6.15)
The awareness of mental modifications is seen to be perishable and insignificant, like a hole in a jar;
in reality, the awareness of modifications is the "I," which is full and imperishable like space.
Whatever is seen internally is called a modification of the intellect;
from those [modifications] which are of the nature of suffering, I am distinct as their direct witness.
For there is indeed a contradiction between the object and the agent when a mental mode (vṛtti) illuminates itself;
and it is certain that this is so because it would involve the conceptual complexity (gaurava) of postulating an infinite series of mental modes. 2.6.18.
Likewise, by means of joy, sorrow, fear, anger, greed, delusion, and pride;
and by means of hatred, conceit, miserliness, sleep, laziness, longing, and so forth.
My intellect, filled with both merit and demerit, consists entirely of suffering;
it reveals itself to me just as a diseased eye reveals itself to a person afflicted by the sun.
I am all-pervading, peaceful, the pure mass of the Supreme Self,
the inconceivable sky of pure consciousness, the inexhaustible mirror of the universe.
It is stainless, without support, devoid of qualities, free from affliction, and without distinction from that which is of its own kind; it is the illuminator of all objects.

One should contemplate: "I am [all this]," because of the non-difference consisting in the absence of heterogeneity among Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others, down to the stationary objects, all of which are sentient. 2.6.23.
I and other persons are of the nature of pure consciousness and space;
therefore, it is proclaimed in the Vedas that "I am indeed the one Self alone."
Seeing thus, the yogi should worship the universe with his own enjoyments;
this is also declared to be the yoga of the self, as taught in the Śruti for the Sāṅkhya-yogins.
Seeing the Self abiding in all beings and all beings in the Self,
he who sacrifices to the Self attains self-sovereignty, perceiving them all as equal.
Thus, even by Manu, self-sacrifice has been declared as a limb of knowledge;
therefore, [one should practice] through the gift of fearlessness and the honoring of one's own enjoyments and so forth.
Honoring all living beings, one should contemplate the Self;
through this, attachment to the enjoyments of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others is abandoned.

Therefore, by means of the vision of their own equality, the yogi should contemplate that equality [of all things] at the time of origination and dissolution, in all states, and at all times. (ViS 2.6.29)
Since all possess a single uniform nature, how could there be passion and the like in the observer?
Even Viṣṇu and the others, though they enjoy great sovereignty, do not possess anything more [than this].
Therefore, I have had enough of those powers which are dear to the undiscriminating,
and of qualities, actions, and so forth— whatever may appear to be superior to my own self.
For that purpose the world exerts itself; I do not see anything superior for myself, nor do I see anything inferior, such that I would fear transgression. (ViSs 2.6.32)
With the hope of conquering them, I shall strive as if for the gods to conquer the Daityas;
and just as I am, so too are all others, from Brahmā down to the inhabitants of hell.
They are seen with love as if they were one's own self, like fathers, brothers, sons, and so forth;
who then is the lord and who is the subject? Who is superior, or even who is inferior?
"The scripture states that from the perception of difference in what is non-different, there arises fear of death;
[yet] within the space of consciousness, which is uniform in nature, there appear forms such as the Lord and the non-Lord."
For every apparent difference in form is unreal, like the various forms seen in a crystal;
by means of the forms of cognitions, the single Person is perceived as if it were manifold.
Like a magician assuming many forms through shapes such as the skin of a wolf, you,
who possess various forms, have embraced me, who am formless.
For it is Māyā alone, as she dances, that deludes all the intellects of men;
the apparent diversity among men arises from the diversity of their intellects, just as the diversity of reflections of the sun arises from the diversity of the waters.
And the distinction of space arises from the divisions of jars and the like, appearing in the form of apertures;
therefore, it is pure, awakened, liberated, ever-present, and immutable.
In that regard, the notion of "I" and "another," as well as the perception of enemies, friends, and so forth, is false—
whether with respect to Brahman, Īśa, Hari, Indra, or likewise the entire multitude of living beings.
The distinction between superior, inferior, and middling is false, being produced by illusion (māyā);
for since the self consists of the three qualities (triguṇa) of illusion, it also possesses a threefold nature.
Indeed, this threefold division into superior, inferior, and middling does not exist by its own nature;
just as it is with the body, so it is elsewhere—this light of consciousness is immutable.
For there is only a difference between the internal and the external in terms of manifestation and non-manifestation;
likewise, other persons also do not differ, whether bound or liberated. 2.6.43.
And because there is no distinction between the Lord and the individual soul, I have no personal goal [to pursue];
therefore, the noble Great Sleep alone is my beloved, for it removes the experience of suffering.
Although my reflection appears in the mirror of consciousness within the minds of those who are foolish, unvirtuous, and devoid of wisdom, it is nonetheless unpleasant to them.
In reality, it does not lead to any fault; nevertheless, it must indeed be abandoned.
For its status as something to be relinquished is established by one's own experience, owing to its very nature.
Just as no one desires to see the deformity of another,
so this virtuous woman, having attributed her own faults to her husband, feels remorse.
Seeing her husband free from fault, the devoted wife herself becomes faultless;
likewise, even though there is a difference in her forms, I am always of one single form.

Whether she is eating or not eating—she who is for my sake alone and goes nowhere else—how wonderful it is that her nature remains uniform, whether in states of union with or separation from limiting conditions! ViSs_2,6.49.
Just as in a stainless mirror, so in my mirror of the sky of consciousness,
the defects residing in the perception of the visible world appear directly to the Lord who is their witness.
Delusion and other such defects do not exist in me, just as there is no defect in the light of the sun;
having abandoned their own selves bound by sufferings, they have attained my state.
One is released from the bondage of suffering; for me, there is neither liberation nor bondage.
In the immutable, unattached, conscious ether, there is merely the reflection of the intellect and its suffering.
Any other bondage that takes the form of enjoyment is also false upon the mirror of consciousness;
it is the witness of the three states beginning with waking, yet remains devoid of them.
I am Pūrṇa, the Sun of Consciousness, devoid of rising and setting;
the universe is not real within me, pure awareness, any more than a face reflected in a mirror.

And because it is not perceived externally or internally during states such as deep sleep, even though the all-pervading Self— whether in me or in another person— is an experience that is pure and omnipresent.

That which appears as a transformation (vivarta) is so because its nature consists of a reflection in the intellect, like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell; therefore, the entire universe does not cause any defect in Me.
Just as water exists in a mirage, and likewise cities and such in the sky,
so too this universe does not exist at all within me, the eternal, throughout the three periods of time.
Let it exist elsewhere, or let it not exist; what does that matter to me regarding the intellect and so forth?
Everything resides in me as it does in space, and I am everywhere like the sky.
Everything is not in me, nor am I everywhere; yet, like space, I am not without being smeared [by it].
Precisely for this reason, through the non-differentiation known as "non-separation," I am like milk and water.
The supreme sages sing that this entire universe is of the nature of consciousness:
"The world is mine, because it exists for my sake, just like the body and the pleasure of myself. (ViSs 2.6.60)
The notion that "others are like me" or "this belongs to me alone" is an error;
in reality, nothing belongs to anyone at all, due to the nature of deviation.
Since ownership is unstable, like a traveler’s lodging-house, there exists here only one thing:
pure consciousness alone, which is stainless, void, and untainted.
Therein, subtler than the subtlest, neither the world nor the activity of the world is seen;
rather, there is only the succession of one's own respective cognitions, enriched by all that is visible.
Having attained its reflection in the great mirror of the circle of consciousness,
the sky remains everywhere— manifest in some places and subtle in others.
Just as it may be, the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) resides both in the location of the intellect and elsewhere;
since the entire universe consists of the space of consciousness, therefore the intellect is here and there.
Wandering here and there, it manifests like a jar or other objects in the sun;
[it manifests] all things such as merit and demerit, birth and death, pleasure and pain, and so forth.
Even while awake, my birth and so forth are as false as a dream;
the notion of the consciousness's birth and destruction arises from its association with and dissociation from the visible world.
Just as the moon appears or does not appear due to the defects of its manifestation or non-manifestation, so too,
during the great deep sleep [of the ultimate state], the momentary and fragile cognitions are like a continuous stream of the bad dreams of existence, birth, and death.
I see myself as untainted by them; for what difference does it make whether the thick clouds of the sun have vanished?
Thus meditating constantly with a one-pointed mind,
the wise person realizes the reality of the Self in its form that is beyond the reach of speech.
If the mind abandons its own pure and tranquil nature for even a moment,
then at that very instant the sense-faculties become agitated due to the residual impressions of the perceptible world.
There, he should repeatedly strike down the risen and unrisen enemies of the senses with the very thunderbolt of solitude, just as Indra strikes the mountains.
Thus ends the chapter on the method of Rājayoga in the *Sāṅkhyasāra* composed by the venerable Vijñānabhikṣu.
Now begins the seventh chapter:
The characteristics of one who has realized the Self and is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
I shall explain clearly that by which there may be an examination of knowledge and ignorance.
Whether through hearing or even through reflection, if one acts otherwise due to the delusion of self-knowledge,
one may treat an ignorant person as a guru; thus, even one who possesses knowledge may become a conceited knower.
The characteristics of knowledge consist in sovereignty, the knowledge of the future, and so forth;
for even without these, liberation has been declared by the author of the *Yogabhāṣya*.

Vedic and Smārta statements concerning those possessed of knowledge who partake in liberation are indeed recorded here as indicators (lakṣaka) for the sake of generating supreme confidence. (ViS 2.7.4)
When for the one who perceives all beings have become the Self alone,
then what delusion and what sorrow can there be for him who beholds this oneness?
He who is without attachment everywhere, and who neither rejoices nor feels aversion upon encountering whatever is auspicious or inauspicious— his wisdom is firmly established.
Just as the ever-moving wind does not forget its course anywhere,
so too the intellect of the wise does not forget pure consciousness, having realized it as the indubitable reality.
He whose facial radiance neither rises nor sets in joy or sorrow,
remaining exactly as it was before, is called one liberated while living.
He who remains awake while in the state of deep sleep, for whom no waking state exists,
and whose consciousness is free from latent impressions— he is called liberated while living.
Even while acting in accordance with passion, hatred, fear, and the like,
he who is as utterly transparent as the inner sky is called one liberated while living.
He whose state of being is not characterized by egoism, and whose intellect is not stained—
whether he is acting or not acting— he is called liberated while living.
Even when the sun has become cool, even when the lunar orb is excessively hot,
and even when fire grows downward, one who is liberated while living does not have another thought.
"These powers constantly manifest here from the conscious self"—
one who knows this feels no curiosity toward its wondrous webs.
A woman devoted to another man, even while busy with household chores,
relishes within herself that very elixir of union with a man.
Thus, when the wise person has attained rest in the supreme, pure reality,
they savor that very state within, even while engaged in external worldly activity.
He who is always absorbed in the inner self, always inward-turned and happy, profound and serene like a great lake within a mountain; // ViSs_2,7.16 //
Unagitated by the flavor of supreme bliss, he rejoices through his own self in the Self;
having renounced all actions, he is eternally joyful and free from affliction.
He is stained neither by merit nor by evil, nor even by anything else;
he is clothed in whatever [garment] and fed by whatever [food].
And wherever he may sleep, he shines like a sovereign emperor,
though he has no desire for the social classes, duties, stages of life, conduct, scriptures, or the methods of mantras.
He emerges from the web of the world like a lion from a cage;
he is beyond the reach of words and is no longer seen by the eye of desire for sense objects.
He attained an indescribable splendor, like the sky in autumn;
he was beyond praise and beyond salutation, devoid of the worship due to those worthy of honor.
Whether joined with or separated from the methods and sequences of right conduct—
this indeed is the sole characteristic of that which is formless,
having attained the cessation of the long wandering of saṃsāra through complete peace.
That is, for whomever there is a daily and skillful attenuation of the calamities of passion, anger, despondency, greed, and delusion.
For one who is established in repose in the Fourth State and has turned back from the ocean of existence,
there is no purpose served by what is done or not done, nor by the delusions of the Śrutis and Smṛtis.
Whether he casts off his body at a sacred ford or in the house of an outcaste,
at the moment of attaining knowledge, he whose heart is stainless is indeed liberated.
Liberation is not on the back of the sky, nor in the netherworld, nor upon the surface of the earth;
for according to the scripture, liberation is the cessation of the mind when all desires have come to an end.
Having abandoned the state of liberation while living when his own body has been surrendered to time, he enters the state of disembodied liberation, just as the wind enters a state of motionlessness.
For when all mountains and other objects have been reflected therein, the nature of the mirror remains as it is—consisting solely of its own essential form. (ViSs 2.7.27)
When the delusion of the visible world— such as "I," "you," and "the universe"— has been stilled,
there arises that state of absolute oneness (kevalatā) when the Seer remains established in non-seeing.
It is pure consciousness alone, devoid of objects of thought, infinite, undecaying, and auspicious;
it is without beginning, middle, or end, free from mental affliction, and untainted by disease.
Neither empty nor possessing form, neither the object of vision nor the act of seeing—
something indescribable and unmanifest remains.
Thus ends the chapter on liberation while living and supreme liberation in the *Sāṅkhyasāra* composed by the venerable Vijñānabhikṣu.
Thus ends the latter part of the *Sāṅkhyasāra*.
The treatise titled *Sāṅkhyasāra* is complete.
